title: Storing equipment, chemicals and consumables
audience: Cleaners and supervisors responsible for putting away, rotating and checking equipment and chemicals in any cleaning-group business.
learningOutcomes: Wash, dry and position mops, buckets, cloths and dust pans so they are ready for the next job and do not hold stagnant water.
Apply the colour system so that equipment from one zone never moves into another.
Store heavy chemical containers at a safe height and position, labelled and closed.
Rotate stock so older product is used first.
Keep fire exits and walkways clear of stored items.

instruction.heading: What the storage area is for
instruction.body: The store is where equipment, chemicals and consumables spend most of their time, and it is where many incidents begin: a leaking container on a shelf, a mop left in a bucket for days, or a fire exit blocked by a stack of cartons. A clean, tidy and odour-free store reduces accidents, extends the life of equipment, and keeps clean areas separate from dirty ones. The source states that the store must be free of smells and clutter, and that rubbish is removed from it.

instruction.heading: Washing and drying equipment
instruction.body: Wash mops, buckets and cloths after each use. Hang mop heads head up so they dry without holding stagnant water. Store buckets upside down with cloths hung over the top to air-dry. Wash and dry dust pans, and store them in their colour group. Buffing pads are washed and hung to dry, and buffers are not stored with a pad or base plate still fitted. Gloves used for washroom work are washed and kept in their own colour group.

instruction.heading: Colour coding as a control
instruction.body: Colour coding separates equipment by zone so that a cloth used on a toilet never travels to a kitchen or office surface. The source gives the example of all red cloths stored together and all blue buckets together. The colour-to-zone map is set by your business, so use the map it gives you rather than a guess. Keep each colour in its own place and check the groupings at every restock.

instruction.heading: Chemical storage rules
instruction.body: Store heavy containers on the floor or below chest height, slightly away from walls, following the label and safety data sheet. Keep the products you use most within easy reach, and rotate stock so older containers are used first. Every container is labelled and has its lid securely fitted or its trigger switched off. Fire exits are kept clear at all times. Store a product only where its SDS is on file, as set out in “Chemical competency: reading labels and safety data sheets”.

instruction.heading: Protective clothing and the end-of-shift check
instruction.body: Wear the protective clothing your business requires when you handle chemicals, machines or consumables in the store. At the end of the shift, confirm the store is clear of rubbish, the colour groups are correct, the chemicals are in their positions and fire exits are open. Record any defect you cannot fix, so the next person knows about it.

procedure: Remove rubbish and waste from the store before you put anything away.
Wash and dry buckets, cloths, dusters and dust pans. Hang mop heads head up and store buckets upside down.
Put each item in its colour group and return it to its zone position.
Place heavy chemical containers on the floor or below chest height, slightly away from walls.
Check each chemical is labelled, closed or triggered off, and has its SDS on file.
Rotate stock: move older product forward and place new stock behind it.
Confirm fire exits and walkways are clear, close the store, and log any defect you cannot fix.

workedExamples.situation: A store has mop heads standing in buckets, cloths in a heap on the floor, and a five-litre drum on a top shelf beside the fire exit.
workedExamples.reasoning: Clear the fire exit first, because a blocked exit is a life-safety issue. Then move the drum to floor level away from the wall, hang the mop heads head up, turn the buckets upside down, and hang the cloths to dry. Check the drum's label and lid, and record the store condition.

workedExamples.situation: A new team member puts the red toilet cloths next to the blue kitchen cloths, saying the colours are close enough.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the risk, and what is the fix?
workedExamples.reasoning: The colour system exists to keep washroom materials away from clean areas. Mixing the groups defeats the control, even if the cloths look clean. Separate them, check the colour map with the supervisor, and brief the team again at the next meeting.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves for handling chemical containers and cleaning equipment.
Protective clothing as required by the business.
Colour-coded racks, hooks and bins for each zone.
Labelled containers with secure lids or triggers.
Wash and drying area with a hanging rack for cloths.
Refuse bags for rubbish removal from the store.

commonErrors.error: Storing mop heads face down in a bucket or on the floor.
commonErrors.prevention: Hang or stand mop heads head up in a holder so they air-dry.

commonErrors.error: Placing a heavy drum on a high shelf because the floor space is needed.
commonErrors.prevention: Heavy containers go on the floor or below chest height, away from walls.

commonErrors.error: Keeping an unlabelled spray bottle on a shelf.
commonErrors.prevention: Label it or set it aside. Unlabelled product is not stored.

commonErrors.error: Stacking boxes or bins where they block a fire exit.
commonErrors.prevention: Fire exits and walkways are kept clear at all times, and defects are logged.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The national model position requires a register of hazardous chemicals stored at the workplace, kept up to date and readily accessible, with a current SDS for each listed chemical.
Fire exit and egress requirements come from building and fire rules that differ between states and territories. The working rule here is simple: an exit is never blocked.
Lift heavy containers from the floor or below chest height where you can, using the business's manual handling procedure.

qualityStandard: Store free of rubbish, with no smells and no clutter.
All items stored by colour group in their zone positions.
Heavy chemical containers on the floor or below chest height, away from walls.
Every container labelled and closed or triggered off, with its SDS on file.
Fire exits and walkways clear, and stock rotated.
documentationEvidence: Store inspection record with date, time and checks completed.
Stock rotation record showing the date of stock received and used.
Defect log entry for any item or fixture that could not be fixed on the spot.
summary: Clean, dry and colour-grouped equipment goes back to its place.
Mop heads head up, buckets upside down, cloths hung over to dry.
Heavy chemicals sit low and away from walls, labelled and closed.
Fire exits are never blocked, and stock is rotated oldest first.

knowledgeChecks.question: A 5-litre chemical container needs to be stored. Where is the safest place?
options: On the top shelf, to keep it out of the way and within easy reach
Against the wall at eye level, for quick access and near the sink
On the floor or below chest height, slightly away from the walls

knowledgeChecks.question: Why are cloths and buckets colour coded?
options: To prevent materials from one zone, such as toilets, moving into clean areas
Colour is decorative and matches the uniform and suits the whole site
To show which products are the strongest for each job and the cost of each product

knowledgeChecks.question: You find a fire exit partly blocked by stock in the store. What is the right action?
options: Leave it until the stock has been used
Clear the exit now and log the defect
Stack more stock beside it to keep the area tidy
